candidates.name: gtab (Google Trends Anchor Bank)
candidates.what_it_holds: Python library (`gtab/` package, pip-installable) implementing the anchor-bank method from the CIKM 2020 paper 'Google Trends anchor bank (GTAB): a method for smooth, calibrated, and comparable time series'. Solves the 5-term-comparison limit and integer-rounding problem in raw Google Trends by binary-searching a pre-computed 'anchor bank' of reference queries to produce calibrated, comparable-across-time-and-geography absolute popularity values (with error bounds), instead of the 0-100 relative index. Repo includes example notebooks, CLI, MIT license, 217 commits.
candidates.why_useful: Directly addresses CONTEXT.md gap #4 (point-in-time/anchored Google Trends) and #17 (anchored Google Trends / gtab named explicitly). Our own past test found raw Trends-as-pulled fails (0/162, renormalization issue) — gtab is the standard fix for exactly that renormalization problem, since it makes pulls comparable across different query dates and regions, which raw pytrends cannot. Worth re-testing travel/ABNB/competitor terms through gtab before concluding Trends is dead.
candidates.time_coverage: as far back as Google Trends itself (2004-present), calibrated via anchor queries
candidates.size_hint: small code package + anchor-candidate query lists; no large committed dataset
candidates.last_activity: not precisely dated from page; 217 commits, actively referenced/cited academic package
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: We hold raw (non-point-in-time) Google Trends for 9 terms; this is a different, calibrated acquisition method, not a duplicate.

candidates.name: trendecon
candidates.what_it_holds: R package (source in /R, vignettes, tests, GitHub Actions CI) that queries Google Trends multiple times across daily/weekly/monthly windows via gtrendsR and harmonizes/rescales the results into a single robust daily time series, avoiding the noise and non-comparability of single raw pulls. Companion live site trendecon.org publishes daily-updated Swiss economic-sentiment indicators built this way (used during COVID for high-frequency nowcasting per Eichenauer et al. 2022, Economic Inquiry). GPL-3.0, 267 commits, active CI.
candidates.why_useful: A second, independently-published fix for the exact renormalization/comparability problem that killed our raw-Trends test (gap #17: 'anchored Google Trends'). The method (not the Swiss-specific site) is directly reusable on any keyword list, including travel/short-term-rental/consumer terms relevant to ABNB nights and consumer strength.
candidates.geography: method is geography-agnostic; the live demo site is Switzerland-specific
candidates.time_coverage: daily series constructible back to 2004 (Trends limit)
candidates.size_hint: R package, no large committed dataset in the repo itself
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: None — new method, not in current holdings.

candidates.name: longtrends
candidates.what_it_holds: Small Python package (pyproject.toml/setup.py, single module) that automates overlapping Google Trends requests and rescales the overlaps to stitch together a single long-run time series beyond the ~5-year/260-week window a single pytrends call returns. No committed dataset; user supplies keywords/date ranges.
candidates.why_useful: Cheap, minimal-dependency way to get a longer, internally-consistent history for any travel/ABNB-adjacent search term (gap #4: historical/point-in-time trends), complementary to gtab (which calibrates absolute level rather than just stitching length).
candidates.time_coverage: as far back as Google Trends goes, stitched
candidates.size_hint: code only, 5 commits, 16 stars, 2 forks — small/lightly maintained
candidates.last_activity: minimal recent activity per repo page
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: None — new stitching method not in current holdings.

candidates.name: trendspyg
candidates.what_it_holds: Actively maintained Python library + CLI (successor-style to pytrends, now that pytrends is archived) for interest-over-time, interest-by-region, related queries, and multi-property (YouTube/News/Images/Shopping) Trends data. New in v1.3.0: opt-in local SQLite archiving so repeated fetches build a self-owned historical/point-in-time snapshot store going forward (cannot backfill past data Google no longer serves). MIT license, v1.8.0, 50 stars/7 forks, active development.
candidates.why_useful: Practical tool for building a going-forward point-in-time Trends vintage register (gap #4) cheaply, and a maintained replacement now that the original pytrends is archived/read-only.
candidates.time_coverage: forward-looking archive only; no historical backfill
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Functional replacement for our existing (non-point-in-time) Trends pull method.

candidates.name: pytrends
candidates.what_it_holds: The original, most widely used unofficial Python client for Google Trends (interest over time, by region, related topics/queries, realtime/trending searches, top charts). 3.7k stars, 889 forks, 635 commits, 136 open issues. Archived/read-only by the owner on 17 Apr 2025 — no longer maintained.
candidates.why_useful: This is almost certainly the tool underlying our existing 9-term Trends pull (already tested and found not to beat naive). Flagging mainly because it is now archived — any new Trends work should move to a maintained fork (trendspyg, pytrends-modern) or the anchored gtab method rather than pytrends itself.
candidates.license: unspecified in fetched view (historically Apache-2.0/MIT-style OSS)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Yes — this is the standard library behind the Google Trends data we already hold and already tested as not useful as pulled.

candidates.name: pytrends-modern
candidates.what_it_holds: Newer Python client billed as 'combining the best features from pytrends, trendspyg, and more' — a post-archival successor client for the same Google Trends endpoints (interest over time/region, related queries).
candidates.why_useful: Alternative maintained client if trendspyg has issues; low incremental value beyond trendspyg since it targets the same underlying data we've already tested.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Yes — same underlying Trends data already tested and found not useful as pulled.

candidates.name: gtrendsR
candidates.what_it_holds: R package providing functions to query and display Google Trends data (interest over time/region/related). This is the R-ecosystem equivalent of pytrends and is the dependency trendecon builds on top of.
candidates.why_useful: Only useful if the team wants an R-based pull path (e.g. to reuse trendecon directly); otherwise duplicative of pytrends-family tools already available in Python.
candidates.license: not confirmed (CRAN package, typically GPL/MIT family)
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: Yes — same underlying Trends data already tested.

candidates.name: gogtrends
candidates.what_it_holds: Unofficial Go-language client for the Google Trends API (interest over time/region, trending/realtime searches). Same endpoints as pytrends, just a different language binding.
candidates.why_useful: No incremental data value for this team's Python/R stack; noted only for completeness.
candidates.last_activity: listed as active on topics page

notes: This session's WebSearch tool had already exhausted its 200-query budget before this scout ran (first three queries returned 'web search was not performed' errors) — all subsequent discovery had to go through WebFetch on GitHub Topics pages (github.com/topics/google-trends pages 1-2, /topics/pytrends, /topics/nowcasting, /topics/gtab) and direct repo-URL guesses. github.com/search?q=... (GitHub's own search UI) started returning HTTP 429 after 1-2 fetches, so keyword-driven repo discovery beyond the topics pages was not possible in this run. Some plausible-sounding repos surfaced only as unverifiable name-guesses (e.g. a 'globaltrends' downloader, a 'DailyTrends' full-daily-series tool, and an NY Fed 'Nowcasting' DFM repo) returned 404 on the exact owner/name I guessed — I dropped these rather than report an unconfirmed URL; a future scout with WebSearch budget or `gh search repos` access should retry 'google trends daily full history' and 'FRBNY nowcasting dynamic factor model' to pin down the correct repo paths. Overall finding for this theme: the tooling landscape (pytrends and its maintained successors trendspyg/pytrends-modern/gogtrends/gtrendsR) is mature but all pull the same relative, non-comparable Trends index CONTEXT.md already says we tested and it failed (0/162 naive). The two genuinely different candidates are gtab (calibrated anchor-bank, absolute comparable values) and trendecon (robustified daily construction via repeated multi-frequency queries) — both are published fixes for the specific renormalization problem behind our failed test, and are the ones worth an actual re-test before writing off Google Trends for ABNB nights/ADR nowcasting. Neither produced a committed historical dataset we could just ingest; both are acquisition methods requiring a fresh pull (subject to CLAUDE.md's scraping rule — Google Trends web queries are not on the sanctioned-sources list of Inside Airbnb dumps / fee-panel capture, so a human should confirm pulling via gtab/trendecon counts as in-scope before running it).
